questions.q: Why does this lesson argue a designer can't fully substitute self-review for an independent design review?
options: Because designers are never qualified to evaluate their own work under any circumstances
Because the person who built a design has already made its assumptions feel reasonable to themselves, so a gap they've stopped noticing is often immediately visible to someone seeing the design fresh
Because self-review is forbidden by Salesforce's architect certification program
Because only a Technical Architect is legally permitted to review a design
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as a structural fact about familiarity, not a statement about skill or trust -- an independent reviewer hasn't internalized the design's baked-in assumptions.

questions.q: Which of these is explicitly part of this lesson's review checklist?
options: Whether the design's Apex classes use camelCase or PascalCase naming
Whether every major design decision traces back to an actual, sourced requirement, and what technical debt the design is knowingly taking on
Whether the design was built using Flow instead of Apex, regardless of fit
Whether the designer has more years of experience than the reviewer
questions.explain: Requirements traceability and technical debt visibility are two of the explicit checklist items this lesson lists, tying the review back to Lessons 2 and 11.

questions.q: How does this lesson say review feedback should be framed to stay productive?
options: Around the design's specific trade-offs, with concrete reasoning -- not around the designer's general competence
As vague statements like 'this isn't well thought out' with no further detail
Only as approval or rejection, with no explanation either way
Exclusively in writing, never in a live conversation
questions.explain: The lesson contrasts specific, actionable feedback ('this scalability assumption doesn't account for requirements volume, here's why') with vague, non-actionable statements about competence.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about a review that approves everything without genuinely engaging the checklist?
options: It is the ideal, most efficient form of review
It is a rubber-stamp review that defeats the review's purpose just as thoroughly as a review that turns into an unproductive argument
It guarantees the design has no gaps
It should be the standard approach for experienced designers
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly names this failure mode (rubber-stamping) as undermining the review's value just as much as an unproductive, personal argument would.

questions.q: Why does this lesson insist review must happen before build, not as a formality afterward?
options: Because reviewing after build is always technically impossible
Because fixing a review finding after a feature is already built and deployed usually means rework rather than a quick design adjustment -- the most expensive point to catch a problem
Because build teams are not allowed to see design documents before review
Because post-build review is actually cheaper, which is why it's discouraged
questions.explain: The lesson ties this directly to Lesson 13's performance-timing argument generalized across every quality attribute: catching an issue before build is cheaper than catching it after deployment, when fixing it usually means rework.
